strengths: Well-motivated core idea: enforcing one-to-one concept-latent mappings via supervised training directly targets the 'feature splitting' problem that limits prior unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (e.g., SAeUron), and the paper backs this up with clear mechanistic evidence (feature-importance score histograms showing a single dominant peak vs. dispersed scores, k-NN classification showing the top-1 latent alone nearly matches using all latents).

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical validation: consistent gains over SAeUron and other baselines on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark (9.2% average improvement), sequential/multi-object unlearning (28.4% improvement over 9 objects), adversarial robustness against UnlearnDiffAtk, and a large (96.7%) reduction in hyperparameter search cost due to single-latent steering.

Extensive appendix with numerous ablations (decorrelation loss, global cross-entropy alternative, post-TopK CA loss, multiplier sweeps, from-scratch vs. fine-tuned variants, concept-interference analysis for Dogs vs. Cats) that substantiate design choices and offer transparency about what does and does not work.

The paper is honest about a failure case: single-latent nudity unlearning underperforms SAeUron (47 vs. 18 detections), and the authors report this along with a two-latent variant that fixes it, rather than hiding the limitation.

Practical relevance is demonstrated beyond synthetic benchmarks (NSFW content suppression on I2P), and the method is presented as architecture-agnostic and applicable at inference-time without modifying base model weights.
weaknesses: The method requires concept labels during SAE training, which is a form of added supervision that competing unsupervised methods (e.g., SAeUron) do not need; the paper does not quantify the extra cost or availability constraints of this labeling requirement, nor discuss how much benefit stems purely from supervision vs. the architectural/loss design.

The one-to-one concept-to-latent assumption breaks down for entangled or blended concepts, as shown by the nudity single-latent failure and the noted struggles in Fig. 13/14 with concepts 'blended with styles' (e.g., flames, jellyfish). This suggests the core assumption is not universally valid and the fix (using more latents) is ad hoc rather than principled.

The composite loss (Eq. 6) introduces multiple additional hyperparameters (β, γ, λ) whose tuning is shown to be sensitive (e.g., β=10 causes complete generative collapse per Appendix 6.10); the claimed '96.67% hyperparameter search reduction' pertains only to inference-time multiplier search and omits this upstream training-time tuning burden, which somewhat undercuts the efficiency claim.

FID/generation-quality results are inconsistently reported: the main comparison table (Table 1) omits FID entirely, and FID is only presented in appendix tables (5, 6) for different variant configurations, making it hard to assess quality-fidelity trade-offs for the exact model used in the primary headline comparison.

The paper acknowledges recomputing baseline metrics due to an inconsistency discovered in the public SAeUron implementation; while transparently disclosed, this introduces some uncertainty about exact comparability with previously published numbers and is not independently verifiable by reviewers without access to the corrected code.

There is no explicit, consolidated 'Limitations' section in the main text; limitations are scattered across appendix subsections (nudity, concept interference, multiplier sensitivity), which reduces the visibility and completeness of a critical self-assessment.

The proliferation of model variant names (OS-DC-CA-FT, S-OS-CA-FS, etc.) in the appendix is not clearly defined in the main text, making it difficult for readers to trace exactly which configuration corresponds to the headline 'SAEmnesia' results without cross-referencing multiple tables.

Evaluation is almost entirely on SD v1.x and the UnlearnCanvas/I2P benchmarks; generalization to other diffusion architectures or newer models (e.g., SDXL, diffusion transformers) is not empirically tested, despite the claim of architecture-agnosticism.

strengths: The core idea—using supervised labels during SAE training to explicitly enforce a one-to-one concept-to-latent mapping and thereby counteract feature splitting—is a sensible and reasonably novel extension of prior unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (SAeUron), and is well motivated by the polysemanticity/feature-splitting problem.

The feature-centralization validation (score-distribution histograms, k-NN classification using only the top-scoring latent) provides a fairly convincing mechanistic argument that the supervised training does concentrate concept information into fewer latents.

The paper reports a large number of experiments and ablations (multiple loss variants, from-scratch vs fine-tuned, sequential unlearning, adversarial robustness, nudity removal, appendix heatmaps of class overlap), which shows an effort toward thorough empirical characterization.
Reduced inference-time hyperparameter search (single multiplier per concept vs. combinatorial search over latent subsets) is a genuinely useful practical benefit if the one-to-one mapping holds.
weaknesses: The headline nudity-removal result undermines the paper's central claim: the actual single-latent SAEmnesia model performs worse than the SAeUron baseline it is compared against (47 vs 18 detections, Table 9), and the reported 'state-of-the-art' result (9 detections) is only achieved by a 'SAEmnesia-TOP2' variant that steers two latents instead of one — directly contradicting the paper's core thesis of precise single-latent, one-to-one concept control. This is disclosed only in the appendix and is not adequately foregrounded or reconciled in the main text or conclusion.

The method requires supervised, per-concept labeled training data (paired prompts/images with concept labels), which is a fundamentally different and more expensive setting than the unsupervised baseline (SAeUron) it is primarily compared against. The claimed '96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search' and 'computational efficiency' gains ignore the added cost of constructing labeled concept datasets and running the supervised training/loss (CA + DC + sparsity), making the efficiency comparison somewhat one-sided.

Robustness/disentanglement results are inconsistent across the many trained variants: several fine-tuned/from-scratch variants (e.g., OS-CA-FT with 14 overlapping timesteps in Table 8) actually show worse Dogs-vs-Cats concept overlap than the SAeUron baseline (10), and the appendix disentanglement heatmaps (Figs. 15-16) reveal severe entanglement for the 'Human' class (accuracies as low as 5.9-58.8%), which is not discussed or explained in the main text despite being a clear failure mode.

The main quantitative improvement over the baseline (Table 1: 91.51 vs. 82.29) rests partly on the authors' own claim that they discovered and fixed an inconsistency in the baseline's public metric computation and then 're-computed the metrics themselves' — this self-reported correction is not independently verifiable from the manuscript and raises reproducibility/fairness concerns about the primary comparison.

Generalization is not empirically demonstrated beyond SD v1.5/v1.4; despite claims of being 'architecture agnostic,' no experiments are shown on other T2I backbones (e.g., SDXL, DiT-based models), limiting confidence in the claimed generality.

The attribution of adversarial-robustness numbers in the text ('dropping from 73.30% to 28.30%... state-of-the-art drop from 26.19% to 2.22%') is not clearly tied to specific methods/bars in Fig. 9, making this key robustness claim hard to verify precisely from the text alone.

The approach's reliance on hand-picked, closed concept vocabularies with labeled supervision reduces its applicability to the open-ended, often unanticipated concepts (e.g., novel copyrighted characters, evolving NSFW content) that motivate real-world unlearning use cases, a limitation that is not discussed in the conclusion despite being central to practical significance.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated method: enforcing one-to-one concept-latent mappings via supervised training directly addresses the feature-splitting problem that limits prior unsupervised SAE-based unlearning approaches, and the idea is intuitive and well explained.

Strong quantitative gains on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark (91.51% vs 82.29% baseline average) along with a large (96.67%) reduction in hyperparameter search cost, which is a practically meaningful efficiency claim if reproducible.

Extensive empirical validation: feature-importance score histograms, k-NN classification probing feature centralization, attention/heatmap visualizations, sequential unlearning experiments, adversarial robustness evaluation against UnlearnDiffAtk, and nudity removal on I2P — this breadth strengthens the overall evidentiary case.

Thorough appendix with ablations across many loss variants (CA, DC, global CE, post-TopK), multiplier sensitivity analyses, and per-object/per-class disentanglement heatmaps, supporting reproducibility and transparency about design choices.
Honest limitation reporting, e.g., the concept-interference case (Dogs vs. Cats) and weaker nudity-unlearning performance with a single latent, which is disclosed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The claim that the score-computation inconsistency was 'discovered in the public implementation of SAeUron' and metrics were 'recomputed' raises reproducibility concerns since the corrected procedure and its validation against the original codebase are not described in enough detail to fully verify the reported comparison is fair.

Method requires labeled/paired concept data (prompts with explicit concept structure) during SAE training, which is a nontrivial supervision requirement compared to fully unsupervised baselines like SAeUron; the paper does not deeply analyze sensitivity to label noise or how this generalizes to less-structured, naturally occurring prompt corpora.

Nudity unlearning with a single latent underperforms SAeUron substantially (47 vs 18 detections) and only becomes competitive with a two-latent variant (SAEMNESIA-TOP2, 9 detections); this weakens the generality of the core 'one latent per concept' premise, since more complex/entangled real-world concepts (like nudity, which spans many prompt variants) may not centralize into a single neuron.

Evaluation is entirely restricted to SD v1.4/v1.5 and the UnlearnCanvas/I2P benchmarks; despite claims of architecture-agnosticism, no experiments validate transfer to newer diffusion backbones (e.g., SDXL, DiT-based models), limiting evidence for broader applicability.

The concept-interference analysis (Dogs vs. Cats) shows inconsistent results across variants (e.g., OS-CA-FT has 14 overlapping timesteps, worse than baseline's 10), suggesting the disentanglement benefits are not uniformly realized across all configurations, which is only briefly acknowledged.

Some quantitative comparisons (e.g., Table 1 main results vs. Table 5/6 appendix results) use different model variants (OS-DC-CA vs. others) without fully clarifying which configuration is the 'canonical' SAEMNESIA, creating minor confusion regarding which numbers should be taken as the primary claimed result.

strengths: Introduces a clear, technically sound idea: a supervised SAE training scheme (Concept Assignment loss + Decorrelation loss + sparsity) that explicitly enforces one-to-one concept-to-latent mappings, directly addressing feature splitting/polysemanticity, a well-known weakness of unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (e.g., SAeUron).

Strong, extensive empirical validation: consistent gains over the unsupervised SAE baseline on UnlearnCanvas (UA/IRA/CRA), a large (96.67%) reduction in inference-time hyperparameter search, superior scalability in sequential unlearning (up to 9 objects), and stronger white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial robustness.

Multiple complementary analyses support the central claim of feature centralization: score-distribution histograms (Fig. 4/9), k-NN classification showing near-identical accuracy from a single latent vs. all latents (Fig. 5), and attention-map visualizations (Fig. 7) all converge on the same conclusion.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with SAE training hyperparameters, loss hyperparameter grid search, standard deviations across seeds (Table 5), computational overhead breakdown (Tables 3–4), and many ablation variants (Table 7–9).

Honest and specific limitations section (closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, scalability to thousands of concepts, U-Net-only evaluation) rather than generic boilerplate, and a preliminary cross-backbone (SDXL-Turbo) experiment is reported despite acknowledged evaluation-protocol caveats.

Broad set of additional experiments (held-out concept generalization, sequential style unlearning, per-class disentanglement heatmaps, nudity suppression on I2P) that stress-test the method beyond the main benchmark.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally requires labeled concept supervision at SAE-training time, which is a real practical constraint versus unsupervised baselines; the proposed workaround for novel/unseen concepts (post-hoc scoring analogous to SAeUron) effectively forfeits the paper's central advantage for closed-vocabulary settings, as acknowledged in Limitations.

In the matched-supervision nudity-unlearning setting (single steered latent, same as SAeUron), SAEmnesia actually underperforms SAeUron (47 vs. 18 NudeNet detections); the reported improvement (9 detections) only comes from steering two latents, undercutting the one-to-one mapping claim for entangled/imbalanced concepts like nudity attributes.

The decorrelation constraint operates only across coarse macro-groups (objects vs. styles) rather than within groups, so semantically close concepts (e.g., Dogs vs. Cats) still show latent overlap/interference in several reported variants (Tables 8–11), and this limitation is not resolved within the paper.

Evaluation is concentrated almost entirely on SD v1.5 + UnlearnCanvas; the only cross-architecture test (SDXL-Turbo) is explicitly labeled preliminary, omits CRA, and the authors note the comparison is "noisy" due to classifier domain mismatch, leaving generalization beyond U-Net SD v1.x largely unverified.

Results and ablations are spread across many near-identical model variants (OO-GCE-FS/FT, OS-DC-CA-FS/FT, OS-CA-FS/FT, OS-TK-CA-FS/FT) that are not consistently better than baselines (e.g., OS-CA-FT underperforms SAeUron on Dogs-vs-Cats overlap in Table 11), making it somewhat difficult to identify a single robust configuration without extensive cross-referencing.

No human perceptual evaluation of generation quality/artifacts is conducted; conclusions rely solely on automated ViT classifiers and FID, which may not fully capture qualitative degradation visible in some qualitative grids (e.g., flames/jellyfish noted as failure cases).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and real problem in SAE-based concept unlearning: feature splitting/polysemanticity, which causes concepts to be distributed across many latents in unsupervised SAEs and makes precise erasure hard.

The supervised concept-assignment (CA) and decorrelation (DC) losses are a reasonably clean and interpretable mechanism to enforce one-to-one concept-latent mappings, and the paper provides direct evidence of 'feature centralization' via feature-importance score histograms (Fig. 4, 9) and k-NN probing (Fig. 5) showing that a single latent captures nearly all discriminative information for a concept.

Extensive empirical evaluation beyond the core UnlearnCanvas comparison: sequential/incremental unlearning (Fig. 8), white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial robustness (Table 2), nudity suppression on I2P, held-out/unseen concept generalization (Table 17), a preliminary cross-backbone test on SDXL-Turbo (Table 12), and a systematic hyperparameter/ablation study (multiple SAE variants in Tables 7-9), which together provide a fairly thorough picture of the method's behavior.

Reasonable practical efficiency argument: the one-to-one mapping removes the need for a combinatorial search over latent subsets, reducing search cost relative to the unsupervised SAeUron baseline (with concrete numbers backing the 96.67% claim), and Table 4 shows inference overhead is not worse than the unsupervised baseline.

The limitations section is candid, explicitly flagging the closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group (semantically similar) interference, and scalability concerns with growing concept counts, and the appendix reports a case (nudity unlearning) where the default single-latent configuration underperforms and needs a two-latent variant to be competitive, rather than hiding this negative result.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'effective NSFW suppression' is weaker than presented in the abstract: the primary SAEmnesia configuration (single steered latent) actually performs worse than the unsupervised SAeUron baseline (47 vs 18 detections, Table 13) on the I2P nudity benchmark, and only a non-default two-latent variant (SAEmnesia-TOP2) beats it; this undercuts the generality of the one-concept-one-latent design that is the paper's central selling point.

The method fundamentally requires labeled concept data during SAE training (prompts/activations tagged per concept), which is a meaningfully stronger supervision requirement than the unsupervised baselines it is compared against; the 'closed-vocabulary' limitation means new concepts either require retraining the SAE or falling back to the same inference-time score-based selection used by the unsupervised comparator, partially eroding the claimed advantage for realistic, evolving concept sets.

Generation quality trade-offs are non-trivial and somewhat underplayed: in Table 15 SAEmnesia's object-unlearning FID (56.15) is markedly worse than several non-SAE baselines (e.g., UCE at 5.1), and this is not discussed in the main text despite being an important quality/diversity metric.

Within-group interference (e.g., the Dogs-vs-Cats overlap case) remains unresolved and is shown in the appendix to sometimes be worse than the unsupervised baseline for certain model variants (Table 11, OS-CA-FT), suggesting the decorrelation constraint does not reliably fix a known failure mode the paper itself highlights as motivation.

A fairly large number of model variants were explored (Tables 7-9, 27-configuration grid search) and the best-performing configuration was selected based on validation/benchmark performance; combined with the relatively small and fixed UnlearnCanvas concept set (20 objects/50 styles), there is a risk that reported gains partly reflect configuration selection on the target benchmark rather than a robustly superior mechanism, which the single additional (preliminary, noisy) SDXL-Turbo experiment does not fully allay.

Scalability to realistic open-vocabulary settings (thousands of concepts) is explicitly acknowledged as unresolved, and no experiment tests beyond the 70-concept UnlearnCanvas regime, leaving the practical significance for large-scale deployment uncertain.

strengths: The core idea—supervised SAE training to enforce one-to-one concept-latent mappings—directly addresses the well-documented feature-splitting problem in unsupervised SAE-based unlearning, and the concept assignment + decorrelation loss formulation is a clean, well-motivated extension of prior work (SAeUron).

The empirical evaluation is extensive: UnlearnCanvas benchmark (object and style), sequential unlearning across 9 objects, white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial robustness, I2P nudity suppression, held-out concept generalization, cross-backbone preliminary results (SDXL-Turbo), and a k-NN feature-centralization validation—together forming a fairly convincing multi-angle case for the method's benefits.

Reported gains are consistently in the method's favor and substantial: +9.22 average points over SAeUron on UnlearnCanvas objects, 96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search cost, large gains in sequential unlearning (+28.4%) and adversarial robustness (57.50% vs 34.20% post-attack UA), plus lower FID and smaller memory/storage footprint than most compared baselines (Table 15).

The paper is transparent about limitations (closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, scalability to very large concept sets, U-Net-only evaluation) and includes an appropriate impact statement discussing dual-use risks of unlearning tools.

Good reproducibility support: detailed training/loss hyperparameters, computational overhead breakdown, standard deviations across seeds, and an extensive appendix with additional ablations (global cross-entropy alternative, post-TopK loss variants, multiplier comparisons) that substantiate the design choices.
weaknesses: The supervision requirement is a non-trivial departure from prior unsupervised SAE unlearning and its practical cost/benefit tradeoff is under-analyzed; while the appendix sketches a closed-vocabulary workaround (score-based latent selection without retraining), this fallback essentially reduces to the unsupervised baseline for genuinely novel concepts, undercutting some of the method's advertised advantage for unseen concepts.

Feature centralization is validated mainly via score-based diagnostics (Figure 4, k-NN classification) and qualitative heatmaps (Figure 7), but a more rigorous causal test of monosemanticity (e.g., ablating the assigned latent alone vs. all latents across a large concept set, with statistical significance) is limited; the nudity-unlearning results (Table 13) show the single-latent design actually failing (47 detections, worse than SAeUron's 18) and requiring a 2-latent variant to be competitive, suggesting the one-to-one mapping assumption breaks down for imbalanced/complex concepts.

Evaluation is restricted to SD v1.5/v1.4 U-Net architectures, with only a small, incomplete preliminary experiment on SDX-Turbo (Table 12) that the authors themselves note is noisy and lacks a fair CRA comparison; no results on more modern transformer-based T2I backbones (e.g., FLUX, SD3) despite claiming architecture-agnosticism.

The within-group interference limitation (e.g., Dogs vs. Cats overlap, visible in the class-disentanglement heatmaps Figures 13-14 with several dark-red off-diagonal or diagonal failures such as Human, Towers, Waterfalls) indicates the one-to-one mapping is not robust across all 20 objects, and the paper does not quantify how frequently such interference occurs or propose a validated fix beyond a future-work suggestion.

Comparisons in Table 1/15 mix fine-tuning-based and mechanistic methods with different assumptions (e.g., some modify base weights, others don't), and while this is noted, the paper could better contextualize why closed-form or weight-editing methods (UCE, RECE) sometimes outperform SAEmnesia on specific metrics without adequately explaining the trade-offs beyond efficiency claims.
